newsitem.title: CHINA: China says keeping close eye on U.S. nuclear tests.
newsitem.headline: China says keeping close eye on U.S. nuclear tests.

text.p: China on Thursday called for total adherence to an international ban on nuclear test explosions and warned it was watching closely a controversial series of underground tests by the United States.

Beijing also dismissed U.S. reports that it had become one of the world's main exporters of the equipment needed to make weapons of mass destruction and that it had diverted an imported U.S. supercomputer to military use.

"We stress that all countries should faithfully abide by stipulations in the nuclear test ban treaty," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang when asked to comment on a series of U.S. nuclear tests begun on Wednesday.

The experiments, which are designed to test weapons materials without triggering a nuclear blast, have come under fire from critics who say they violate the spirit if not the letter of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty signed last year.
Some critics said they feared the tests could spur nations such as China and Russia to launch their own underground experiments, which would be difficult to track.
Tang said Beijing had taken notice of the tests, which are being carried out in tunnels deep under the Nevada desert.
"We will certainly pay close attention to this situation," he told a regular news briefing, but did not elaborate.
China itself has come under repeated fire from U.S. critics who accuse Beijing of helping to supply Iran, Pakistan and India with the equipment needed to make weapons of mass destruction.

The charges were bolstered this week by reports in a U.S. newspaper that the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had named China and Russia as the world's premier exporters of such weapons during the second half of 1996.

The Washington Post quoted from an unclassified CIA report prepared for Congress as saying exports from the two nations helped Iran, India and Pakistan develop ballistic missilies, poison gas weapons, or a capability to make nuclear arms.
Such reports were baseless, said Chinese spokesman Tang.
"This is making something out of nothing," he said. "It is a fabrication."

Suspicions that Chinese companies have exported the means to make missiles, chemical weapons or nuclear bombs have been a lingering irritant in sensitive Sino-U.S. ties already strained by disputes over trade, human rights and Taiwan.
U.S. fears have also been raised by allegations that Beijing was using a supercomputer bought from the United States for military ends.

Washington was concerned China might have recently diverted American supercomputers from civilian to military use, prompting Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to raise the issue with Beijing officials this week, the State Department said.

The New York Times on Wednesday quoted U.S. officials as saying they discovered that one supercomputer did not reach its intended destination in Beijing, but was shipped instead to a defence and scientific research institute in Changsha city.

Tang reiterated China's denial of the allegations, saying the high-power computers were imported for such harmless purposes as weather-forecasting and earthquake prevention and were not being used for anything else.
